design_detail: Narrative review, single author (Psychopharmacology 2004;173:234-241), read as the published PDF; the page numbers are the journal's own (pp. 234-241). It aims to estimate, for three historical phases (1970s to early 1990s, mid-1990s, late 1990s to 2002), what share of tablets sold as ecstasy contained MDMA, to report the amount per tablet where measured, and to describe how people who use ecstasy perceived purity (Abstract, p. 234; p. 235). There is no methods section, search, database or inclusion rule. The evidence is arranged in three tables of studies (Table 1, p. 236: seven rows from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s; Table 2, p. 236: nine rows from the mid to late 1990s; Table 3, p. 237: nine rows from the late 1990s to 2002), 25 rows in all (editors' count): 15 laboratory analyses of tablets or capsules, 4 toxicological series of deaths and 6 surveys of what people said about purity. Three series carry the headline estimates (Renfroe, 1986, a Californian anonymous testing laboratory; Spruit, 2001, the Dutch government's Drug Information Monitoring System; Schifano, 2000, forensic laboratories in north-eastern Italy), and the review says so (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238). The rest are small, are a personal communication, or are described only as 'a majority' or 'almost all'. No quantitative synthesis and no intervals.
can_establish: What laboratory analyses published or reported up to 2002 found in tablets and capsules sold as ecstasy (the proportion containing MDMA, its relatives MDA and MDEA, amphetamines or other substances, and the milligrams of MDMA per tablet where measured), as summarized by one author, and how those findings differ by period and place.
cannot_establish: A proportion of tablets sold as ecstasy that contain MDMA in any year or country: none of the cited samples was random, the review gives no intervals, and its estimates are ranges built from different sampling frames (tablets brought in by people who use drugs, amnesty bins, police seizures, a paid testing service). Also anything after 2002; what any person took, how many tablets, or what they felt; and whether the tablets tested resemble the ones people took.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). The cited analyses drew tablets from samples brought in by people who use drugs (the Dutch monitoring service; Renfroe's anonymous mail-in laboratory; the Dancesafe website), amnesty bins at a London dance venue, police seizures (Italy; UK) and a paid testing service (US$100 a pill). The review states that no study used a random sampling procedure (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated: no search, databases or dates. The sources include a personal communication (Ramsey, 2003), a short item in a Czech addiction journal (Palenicek et al., 2002), a website listing and book chapters, none of which can be checked from the review.
sample.selection_effects: The review's own limits (the paragraph beginning 'It should be emphasized that this area is fraught with methodological problems', p. 235; Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 238): no randomized sampling; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or taken from amnesty bins; police seizures of large uniform batches may overstate how often tablets hold MDMA; the paid service probably over-represented atypical drugs; many studies cover one time point and are small. Editors' observations: no search was made, so absent studies cannot be assessed; the three large series dominate the estimates, and one of them (Italy) is built largely on police seizures; the newest data are from 2002.

exposure.measurement: Laboratory analysis of tablets or capsules, as summarized: thin-layer and gas chromatography (Renfroe), a three-stage quick test followed by laboratory analysis of unidentified pills in the Dutch service (p. 236), gas chromatography and infrared spectroscopy (Czech Republic), high-pressure liquid chromatography (Cole et al.); some entries are only statements that 'a majority' or 'almost all' held MDMA. The review does not appraise the methods.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable as doses: the review reports the milligrams of MDMA measured per tablet or capsule (for example 73-102 mg as UK annual averages, 100-150 mg in Italy, 0-152 mg in one Czech set; pp. 239-240), which describe the tablets, not amounts taken. Recorded here only as study conditions.
exposure.polysubstance: The review separates the content of tablets from deliberate polydrug use by people, which it argues is probably a more important confound for research than accidental ingestion of other drugs, without data in this paper (p. 239).

comparison.controls: None: the review compares periods and places, not groups of people.

outcomes.instruments: Laboratory identification and, in some series, measurement of MDMA per tablet; surveys and interviews about perceived purity.
outcomes.validity_norms: Not discussed: detection limits and the accuracy of the quick tests are not given.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Contained MDMA' means MDMA identified in the tablet, alone or mixed; the tables do not apply this uniformly (the Dutch series separates 'MDMA only' from 'mixtures', Renfroe's figure counts 'MDMA or MDA', and the 2002 website figure counts MDMA 'alone or in combination').

analysis.effect_sizes: Percentages as reported by the cited series, with no intervals. Renfroe: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy or similar names held MDMA or MDA (printed as 97%). Dutch service, each year 1993-1996: 48-60% MDMA alone, 12-20% MDEA alone, 2-5% MDA alone, 7-13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or others, 1-4% amphetamine alone, 2-7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA, and 6-17% 'other drugs'; 1997: 44% MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine, 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; 1998: 75% MDMA alone; 1999: 81% (p. 236). North-eastern Italy 1995-2000, at least 20,000 tablets: 85-90% MDMA, 8-10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others; UK 2001, 136 tablets: 100% MDMA; a US website 2002, about 175 tablets: 88% MDMA alone or in combination, 4% MDA or MDE, 4% others, 4% no identifiable drug (Table 3, p. 237). The review's own estimates: 90-98% in the 1980s to early 1990s, 50-80% in the mid to late 1990s (with 5-30% MDA or MDEA and 4-20% others), 80-95% in the late 1990s, near 100% in the early 2000s (p. 238). Amount per tablet: UK annual averages 90-102 mg (1991-1995) and 73-88 mg (1996-2001); Italy mostly 100-150 mg (p. 239); 80 identical white tablets from one 2001 UK seizure 73-89 mg, mean 79 mg; Czech tablets 30-100 mg with outliers of 152 and 0 mg (p. 240).
analysis.selective_reporting: No search or inclusion rule is stated, so selection cannot be assessed. The review identifies the Californian, Dutch and Italian series as the only large ones over time (p. 238) and includes a personal communication and a website listing as evidence for the most recent period.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In the cited analyses most tablets sold as ecstasy held MDMA in every period, but the share ranged from about half to nearly all: lowest in the Netherlands in the mid-1990s (44-60% MDMA alone in a year; 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999), mostly above 85% in north-eastern Italy in 1995-2000 and in the small samples after 1999 (136 of 136 in the UK; about 88% of 175 on a US website). The tablets without MDMA held MDA or MDEA (related drugs), amphetamines, caffeine, ketamine, dextromethorphan, atropine, 4-methylthioamphetamine and others, or nothing active (about 1% in Italy, 4% on the US website). The amount of MDMA varied from none to about 150 mg across samples and, in the one seizure measured, from 73 to 89 mg within a uniform batch.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the purity problem was predominantly a phenomenon of the mid to late 1990s, that non-MDMA tablets are now very infrequent with purity between 90% and 100%, and that high dose tablets are now seen more frequently; the Discussion says the broad validity of using data from people who use ecstasy to estimate the consequences of MDMA is a key finding (p. 239). The text calls its own estimates very approximate (p. 238). The 90-100% for the early 2000s rests on one police-laboratory sample (136 tablets), a personal communication ('almost all') and a self-submitted website sample at 88%; 'high dose tablets now seen more frequently' rests on one mention of occasional high-dose tablets in 1998 and one website listing in 2002 (p. 240), while the review's own UK averages fell between 1991-1995 and 1996-2001 (p. 239).

timeline.event: Californian anonymous testing laboratory: 87 of 89 samples submitted as ecstasy, MDMA, Adam or XTC held MDMA or MDA (Renfroe; as summarized in this review).
Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, 1993-1999: MDMA alone in 44-60% of tablets a year in 1993-1997, 75% in 1998, 81% in 1999 (Spruit; as summarized in this review).
UK forensic laboratory sample of 136 tablets, all containing MDMA (Cole et al.; as summarized in this review).

replication.where_it_stands: A 2004 summary of tablet analyses up to 2002, usable as a second-hand description of that period. Later monitoring data are not in this review. A newer European pill-content study (Vrolijk et al., 2022) is not yet in the library; it would add current years, a defined European sample and milligrams per tablet over time.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PDF carries no funding statement or acknowledgements.
funding.affiliations_note: Single author, Department of Psychology, University of Wales Swansea. The author has published on harms attributed to ecstasy and on polydrug use among people who use it, and 11 of its 59 references are his own work (editors' count), including the suggestion, from studies he ran in 1997 at the University of East London, that poor-quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity (p. 239). The question the review answers, whether research on ecstasy measures MDMA, bears on that work; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: Regular, random or systematically sampled purchases of tablets and powders sold as ecstasy, in defined places and years, analysed quantitatively for every active ingredient (MDMA, related drugs, other drugs and adulterants) and reported with the number of tablets, the sampling frame, the milligrams of MDMA per tablet and the spread within and between batches, so that the share with no MDMA and the spread of the amount can be estimated with intervals.

domains.note: No search, databases, dates or criteria; the sources include a personal communication, a website listing and short newsletter items, and selection cannot be assessed.

No appraisal of analytical methods or sampling beyond two footnotes to Table 2 (samples too small for estimates; a paid sample probably over-representing atypical drugs); figures are repeated as reported and several do not agree between the abstract, tables and text (see reporting issues).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: 11 of the 59 references are the author's own; they are used for perceptions of purity and for the suggestion that poor-quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity (p. 239), not for the tablet-content data, which come from other groups.

Estimates are labelled very approximate and the sampling limits are stated (p. 238), but the abstract's 'high dose tablets now seen more frequently' rests on one website listing, and the serotonin-syndrome risk of high-dose tablets for first-time people is speculation without data (p. 240).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on how often tablets sold as ecstasy contain MDMA
domains.note: Reports of low and of high purity are both given, with the mid-1990s dip described in detail; the explanations offered for the dip (supply of the chemical precursor, the later scheduling of related drugs; pp. 236, 239) are single accounts and are not tested.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS 5.3); the editors' checklist is used. The review is a useful and mostly well-hedged map of what was measured in tablets sold as ecstasy up to 2002 and of why the numbers differ, and it can be cited as a second-hand description of that. It cannot be cited for a population proportion, for any period after 2002, or for the trend in amount per tablet. Every figure should be taken from the primary series (Renfroe, 1986; Spruit, 2001; Schifano, 2000; Cole et al., 2002) once those are read; a claim resting only on this review stays at draft.

key_findings.finding: Abstract: not every tablet sold as ecstasy contained MDMA. The author describes three phases: few problems until the early 1990s; in the mid-1990s a majority still held MDMA while many held MDA, MDEA or amphetamine mixtures and a small share (stated as 4-20% according to survey, time and place) held non-amphetamine drugs such as caffeine, ephedrine, ketamine, paracetamol or placebo; in the late 1990s MDMA rose to around 80-90%; the latest reports suggest 90-100%. Dosage is described as highly variable, with low dose tablets common in the mid-1990s and high dose tablets now seen more frequently.

Earliest data: of 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory in 1972-1985, 610 were MDA or MDMA pills; 89 of these were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy, and all but two held MDMA or MDA (the two exceptions: an amphetamine capsule and an almost empty syringe). Table 1 gives 97% (n = 87). Surveys of what people said in 1987-1995 (US, Australia and UK; 100, 100, 20 and 209 people) reported no or few concerns about purity, and toxicology of 22 deaths and acute toxic reactions (Dowling) and of 7 deaths (Henry et al.) found MDMA, MDEA or MDA in each case, with other drugs in the larger series.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 235); Table 1 (p. 236)

key_findings.finding: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System (Spruit, 2001, as summarized): in each year 1993-1996, around 48-60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12-20% MDEA alone, 2-5% MDA alone, 7-13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or others, 1-4% amphetamine alone and 2-7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held a ring-substituted amphetamine or amphetamine every year, and 6-17% were 'other drugs' (LSD, DOB, ketamine, 2C-B, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone and 18% non-amphetamine drugs, a time the review links to high demand and difficulty obtaining the chemical precursor; MDMA alone rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Samples were mostly brought in by individual people, with a quick test and, for unidentified pills, laboratory analysis.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s, 1st paragraph (begins p. 235; the figures are on p. 236); Table 2, Spruit rows

key_findings.finding: Other mid-1990s analyses were small (13, 25 and 30 tablets in the UK, of which 77%, 64% and 87% held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, often in low or variable amounts; 107 pills in a paid US service, 63% MDMA, MDA or MDEA, with dextromethorphan, caffeine, ephedrine and salicylates among the others) and are called by the review too small for population estimates. Contents other than MDMA, MDA or MDEA included caffeine, amphetamine or ephedrine with caffeine, paracetamol, ketamine, phenylbutanamine, 2C-B and 4-methylthioamphetamine. The review stresses that the large majority of tablets still held MDMA or another ring-substituted amphetamine, and cites a 1996 WHO meeting calling the term ecstasy virtually generic for those drugs.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s, 2nd paragraph (begins p. 236, ends p. 237); Table 2 (p. 236)

key_findings.finding: Late 1990s to 2002 (Table 3): north-eastern Italy, at least 20,000 tablets in 1995-2000, 85-90% MDMA, 8-10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others; Netherlands 1999, 81% MDMA only; Czech Republic, 120 pills, over 80% MDMA only; UK 2001, 136 tablets, 100% MDMA; a US website in 2002, about 175 tablets, 88% MDMA alone or in combination, 4% MDA or MDE, 4% others, 4% no identifiable drug; a London amnesty bin, tablets 'almost all' MDMA (personal communication, 2003).
key_findings.locator: Table 3; MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Australian people interviewed in Perth in 1998-2000 (Hansen et al., 2001) estimated that around one tablet in every four or five was a 'dud', which the review says approximates the more systematic survey data.
key_findings.locator: MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: The review's own rough estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: 90-98% from the 1980s to the early 1990s (the remaining 2-10% generally MDA); 50-80% in the mid to late 1990s (5-30% MDA or MDEA, 4-20% others); 80-95% in the late 1990s; near 100% in the early 2000s. It calls them very approximate, says only three reports involved large samples over an extended time (Renfroe, Spruit, Schifano), that no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure, that most samples came from people who use drugs or from amnesty bins, that police seizures of uniform batches may overstate purity, and that the paid US series probably over-represented atypical drugs.

A substantial minority of tablets held other drugs: 6-18% of Dutch samples in 1993-1997 were 'other drugs' not in the amphetamine class; the review names ketamine (very different effects, possibly distressing if taken unknowingly), 4-methylthioamphetamine ('flatliners', described as highly toxic and implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands, as quoted from Ramsey et al.), atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine and dextromethorphan, and weak substances such as paracetamol, caffeine or placebo. When tablets held MDA or MDEA the review argues people would probably not notice marked differences except possibly in duration.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets comprise other psychopharmacological compounds'; the preceding paragraph on MDA and MDEA

key_findings.finding: Perceptions: the review reports that people interviewed said they could tell occasions when they had taken MDMA from their other experiences, using jaw clenching, tooth grinding, the quality of mood changes and initial nausea to gauge the purity and strength of tablets (Hansen et al., 2001); winter 1997 studies in East London found frequent complaints about poor quality supplies and no neurocognitive impairments, which led the author to suggest that poor quality tablets might protect against neurotoxicity. The review gives no measurement of whether such signs match what a tablet held.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical'

key_findings.finding: Amount per tablet: north-eastern Italy mostly 100-150 mg in 1995-2000; UK annual averages 90-102 mg in 1991-1995, falling to 73-88 mg in 1996-2001 (Cole et al., 2002). Small mid-1990s UK studies found variable and often low amounts: some tablets 100-140 mg, others around 50 mg, some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al.); Czech tablets 30-100 mg with borderline values of 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose); 80 identical-looking white tablets from one 2001 UK seizure ranged 73-89 mg, mean 79 mg. High dose tablets were occasionally found in the Dutch data in 1998 and an American drug website listed a number of them in 2002 (Green et al., 2003); the Dancesafe site listed various high dose examples, but many were at far lower levels or were mixtures. The review says unknown dosage remains a key area of uncertainty. These are measurements of tablets, not amounts to take.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic' (begins p. 239, ends p. 240)

key_findings.finding: Conclusions: the author concludes that unknown contents will always be a problem for people buying any illicit drug but that, for ecstasy, this was mainly a problem of the mid-1990s; earlier ecstasy was a drug of high street purity, its reputation has largely been restored, and the most recent surveys suggest MDMA purity rates of around 90-100%. The review states, without data, that high dose tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time. A 1979 death after 840 mg of MDA powder, which the person and others believed was another drug, is given as an example of the danger of unknown contents.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic' (end) and the paragraph beginning 'To summarize'

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives about 80-90% of tablets holding MDMA in the late 1990s; the Discussion gives about 80-95% for the same period, citing the same two sources (Spruit; Winstock et al.).
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline figure for the late 1990s depends on which part of the paper is read; the Winstock source is a survey of what people said, not an analysis of tablets.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says a small proportion (4-20% according to survey, time and place) held non-amphetamine drugs, and the Discussion repeats 4-20% for the mid to late 1990s, but the Dutch series shows 6-18% (Table 2) or 6-17% a year, and the only 4% in the review is the 2002 website sample (4% others, 4% no identifiable drug).
reporting_issues.consequence: The lower bound of 4% cannot be traced to a mid-1990s source; use the Dutch figures for that period.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says high dose tablets are now seen more frequently. The text supports this only with the Dutch service noting that high dose tablets were occasionally encountered in 1998 and one American website listing a number of high dose tablets in 2002, while the Dancesafe site listed many high dose examples at far lower levels; the review's own UK annual averages fell from 90-102 mg to 73-88 mg.
reporting_issues.consequence: A rising trend in amount per tablet is not shown; the abstract's statement should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says the biochemical evidence shows tablets nearly always contained MDMA before the 1990s. The evidence is 89 samples from one US laboratory (87 holding MDMA or MDA, so MDA is counted), surveys of what people said and short death series.
reporting_issues.consequence: 'MDMA or its relative MDA' is what the figure measures for the 1970s and 1980s, from one laboratory's anonymous submissions.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says 12% of Renfroe's 610 MDA or MDMA samples were submitted as MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy and then says 89 samples; 12% of 610 is about 73, and 89 is about 15%. Table 1 prints 97% for 87 of 89, which is 97.8%.
reporting_issues.consequence: A small slip, but it shows the figures were not checked against the primary paper; figures should be taken from the source.

reporting_issues.issue: Winstock et al. (2001) are described in Table 3 as a questionnaire survey of 1151 'regular/heavy' ecstasy-taking people, in the text as 1151 dance clubbers including numerous experienced people from the harder end of the scene, and in Degenhardt et al. (2010, Table 1) as 1106 readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy.
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample is not reliably described; it is used in the review only for people's reports that supplies improved.

reporting_issues.issue: Palenicek et al. (2002) are dated 1998-2001 in Table 3 and 1998-2002 in the text; the source is a two-page item in a Czech journal and the quotation about 30-100 mg tablets cannot be checked.
reporting_issues.consequence: Dates and amounts from this source are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The Italian series, one of the three used for the headline estimates, is made largely of police seizures in north-eastern Italy, while the review warns that large uniform seized batches may lead to an overestimated level of purity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The review's own caveat applies to its largest late-1990s series; the 85-90% figure may be too high for tablets in circulation.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 234-241 (PDFs/MDMA/Parrott_2004_IsEcstasyMDMA.pdf), full text including the reference list; extracted once with pdftotext; Tables 1-3 (pp. 236-237) and the Discussion pages (pp. 238-240) were checked against 110 dpi renderings of the pages.
